questions.question: How do bufio.Scanner and bufio.Writer work in Go?
questions.title: Bufio Scanner And Writer
questions.direct_answer: Scanner: reads a stream line-by-line (Scan() advances, Text() returns the line). Writer: buffers writes (WriteString accumulates, Flush commits) — batching small writes into large I/O operations.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Scanner: reads a stream line-by-line (Scan() advances, Text() returns the line). Writer: buffers writes (WriteString accumulates, Flush commits) — batching small writes into large I/O operations.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Both, executed:

```go
// Scanner — line-by-line reading
scanner := bufio.NewScanner(strings.NewReader("line one\nline two\nline three\n"))
for scanner.Scan() {
    fmt.Println("scanned:", scanner.Text())
}
// line one, line two, line three — verified

// Writer — buffered writing
var buf strings.Builder
w := bufio.NewWriter(&buf)
w.WriteString("buffered ")
w.WriteString("output\n")
w.Flush()  // without Flush, the data never arrives
fmt.Print(buf.String())  // "buffered output\n" — verified
```

The Scanner pattern: NewScanner(io.Reader) → Scan() returns bool (false at EOF) → Text() returns the current line. It handles line splitting (\n by default; custom split functions for words, CSV, etc.). The loop is the idiom — a for with Scan and a body using Text/Bytes.

The Flush discipline: a bufio.Writer holds a buffer (default 4096 bytes). Writes accumulate; Flush pushes them to the underlying writer. If you forget Flush, partial data stays in the buffer — the classic bug. defer w.Flush() after creating the writer.

The why: batching. A hundred 100-byte writes to a file or network are 100 syscall-sized operations — buffered, they're one 10KB write. The performance difference is an order of magnitude on most systems.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[Scanner] --> SCAN[Scan] --> TEXT[Text] --> LOOP[next line]
    W[Writer] --> WS[WriteString accumulates] --> FL[Flush commits]
    FL --> U[underlying writer]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The Scanner's internal buffer and the line-length limit: Scanner has a fixed 64KB default buffer — a line longer than the limit makes Scan return false with Err(too long). The fix: scanner.Buffer(make([]byte, 1024*1024), 1024*1024) for large lines. The common production bug: log files with huge lines failing silently.

The split functions: Scan() uses SplitFunc — the default ScanLines; bufio.ScanWords, bufio.ScanRunes exist; a custom SplitFunc handles any framing. The Scanner is a general tokenizer over an io.Reader.

The Writer's sizing: NewWriterSize(w, n) for a custom buffer. The trade: larger buffers mean fewer, larger writes (good for throughput) with more memory and latency (data sits until the buffer fills). The TSV of batching — tuned by the actual write pattern.
